lesson.text: Quick memory: what does a trusted adult do? (Listens, keeps you safe and helps.) Today: friendships, how they change, and how to handle pressure from others.
Friendships change as we grow: we move class, find new interests or make new friends. That is normal. Old friends can still be friends, even if you spend less time together.
A healthy friendship feels good: you trust each other, take turns, listen, say sorry and forgive, and can each be yourselves. Both of you can say no, and the other accepts it.

An unhealthy friendship often feels bad. Someone always has to get their way, or puts you down. They leave you out on purpose, or tell you who you cannot play with. You feel you must do things to stay friends.
Falling out happens. Calm down first, then talk: listen, and say how you feel with an 'I' message: 'I feel upset when I'm left out.' Look for a fair compromise, and say sorry if you were wrong.
Peer pressure is feeling pushed to do something because people your age are doing it or want you to. It can be good, like joining a club, or unhealthy, like a dare to break a rule or be unkind.

How to say no: say it clearly ('No, thanks'), and give a reason if you want. Suggest something else, or walk away, and stay with friends who respect you. If the pressure keeps coming, tell a trusted adult.
Try it in the world: build a friendship bench where anyone can sit if they want someone to play with. For real: practise saying no in a firm, friendly voice, and ask someone new to join your game.

items: they leave you out on purpose
you can say no and they listen
they say who you cannot play with
exercises.hint: How would each one make you feel?
exercises.explain: Healthy: taking turns, a no that is heard, saying sorry and forgiving. Unhealthy: leaving out, putting down, controlling who you play with.

exercises.prompt: It is normal for friendships to change as we grow.
exercises.hint: Do people's interests and classes change?
exercises.explain: True: friendships change, and that is normal. You can still be kind to old friends.

exercises.hint: Peers are people your own age.
choices: feeling pushed to do something by others
a way to pump up a ball
exercises.explain: Peer pressure is feeling pushed to do something because people your age are doing it or want you to.

exercises.prompt: Which is a clear, friendly way to say no?
exercises.hint: A good no is clear, and can suggest something else.
choices: No, thanks. Let's play football instead.
say yes to keep them happy
exercises.explain: 'No, thanks. Let's play football instead.' It is clear and friendly, and offers something else.

exercises.prompt: Put making up after a falling out in order.
exercises.hint: Can you listen well while you are angry?
items: say how you feel with an 'I' message
exercises.explain: Calm down, listen, say how you feel with an 'I' message, then find a fair compromise.

exercises.hint: An 'I' message starts with how you feel.
choices: I feel upset when I'm left out.
exercises.explain: 'I feel upset when I'm left out.' It says how you feel without blaming, so the other person can listen.

exercises.hint: Can friends ever push you to do something good?
exercises.explain: False: it can be good, like friends cheering you on to join a club or try a new sport.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: each gives a little to agree
being pushed by others your age
exercises.hint: Think about when you would use each one.
exercises.explain: Peer pressure: being pushed. Compromise: each gives a little. An 'I' message: saying how you feel. Upstander: someone who helps.

exercises.prompt: A friend dares you to climb a fence into a building site. What should you do?
exercises.hint: Building sites are dangerous. Whose safety matters most?
choices: say no, walk away and tell a grown-up
exercises.explain: Say no, walk away and tell a grown-up: a real friend would not want you to get hurt.

exercises.prompt: Good peer pressure or unhealthy peer pressure?
items: friends ask you to join a club
a dare to take something from a shop
your team cheers you on to try
being told to leave someone out
friends invite you to learn a dance
being pushed to tell a secret
exercises.hint: Does it help you, or could it hurt you or someone else?
exercises.explain: Good: joining a club, being cheered on, learning a dance. Unhealthy: taking things, leaving people out, telling secrets.

exercises.prompt: Zara's friend says, 'If you play with Mimi, you can't be my friend.' What kind of friendship is this?
exercises.hint: Should a friend decide who you play with?
choices: unhealthy: friends don't choose your friends
healthy, because they care about you
exercises.explain: Unhealthy: a real friend lets you play with others too.

exercises.prompt: A good friend will accept it when you say no.
exercises.explain: True: a good friend respects your no, even if they are disappointed. If someone keeps pushing after you say no, that is pressure, not friendship.

exercises.prompt: Someone online keeps asking you to send a photo of yourself. What should you do?
exercises.hint: Is it safe to keep this to yourself?
choices: stop replying, and tell a trusted adult
delete the app and tell no one
exercises.explain: Stop replying and tell a trusted adult. You never have to send photos, and it is never your fault.

exercises.prompt: Your group is laughing at a new pupil. What could an upstander do?
choices: invite them to join in, and tell an adult
exercises.explain: Invite the new pupil to join in, and tell an adult if the unkindness goes on.

exercises.prompt: If a friendship feels bad most of the time, it is OK to spend less time with that person.
exercises.hint: Do you have to stay in a friendship that makes you unhappy?
exercises.explain: True: you can spend more time with people who treat you kindly, and still be polite to the other person. If it keeps upsetting you, tell a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: Two friends want to play different games. What is a fair compromise?
exercises.hint: A compromise means each person gives a little.
choices: play one game first, then the other
exercises.explain: Play one game first, then the other: both friends get something they want. Toss a coin to choose which goes first, so the start is fair too.

exercises.prompt: Turn each blaming message into an 'I' message.
matches: I feel sad when I'm not heard.
I feel upset when I'm left out.
I feel cross when I miss a go.
exercises.hint: An 'I' message says how you feel and when, without blaming.
exercises.explain: Left out: 'I feel upset when I'm left out.' Not listened to: 'I feel sad when I'm not heard.' A missed turn: 'I feel cross when I miss a go.' Each one lets the other person listen, not argue.

exercises.prompt: Friends dare you to do something you feel is wrong. Put a strong answer in order.
items: Walk away if they keep on.
Tell a trusted adult if it keeps happening.
exercises.hint: Start with a clear no. A trusted adult helps when the pressure does not stop.
exercises.explain: Say 'No, thanks' clearly, then suggest something else. If they keep on, walk away and stay with friends who respect you. If the pressure keeps coming, tell a trusted adult.
